articles.title: What Teamsters Class Solidarity Looks Like
articles.content_excerpt: (Who Moves America) I was at a Crotona Park barbecue in the South Bronx to celebrate my wife’s nephew, who was going off to a trade school after graduating high school. The family barbecue included a cross section of union members, among them electricians, hotel workers, Teamsters — not a strange amalgam, thanks to New York’s high union density . It’s often only in TV shows that you see a tight-knit group of friends from vastly different class backgrounds hanging out together. In real life, we can’t curate a social circle of people from disparate backgrounds with the same ease you assemble an eclectic wardrobe from a thrift store. articles.title: The Jewish Socialists Who Fought the Tsar and Zionism
articles.author: Molly Crabapple
articles.content_excerpt: Jewish socialist intellectuals founded the Bund in the Russian Empire in 1897, and it soon became a mass organization of the Jewish working class — a working class confined by law to the Pale of Settlement. From its inception, the Bund and the socialist politics it represented struggled against capitalists and autocrats alongside non-Jewish socialist comrades. It also competed bitterly with its Jewish rivals: Orthodox traditionalists, Zionists, and Bolsheviks. Amid repression and revolution, the story of the Jews of the western Russian Empire diverges. Huge numbers emigrated to the Americas, and more than anywhere to New York City, where they built a Yiddish-speaking socialist world whose inheritors are in many ways today’s anti-Zionist socialist Jews. articles.title: M*A*S*H is an Antiwar Masterpiece
articles.author: Midwestern Socialist -- Chicago DSA
articles.content_excerpt: In December of last year, I started watching the television show M*A*S*H , which ran on CBS from 1972 to 1983. As a history nerd with a penchant for old TV shows I quickly became obsessed, watching every single episode in under six months. For those unfamiliar, the show is a comedy-drama following the exploits of the personnel serving at the 4077th Mobile Army Surgical Hospital (M*A*S*H) during the Korean War (1950-1953). Intended as an allegory for the Vietnam War, the show tapped into the intense anti-war and anti-institutional sentiment of broad swaths of the American public of the time. The show is unapologetically anti-war and progressive, unrelenting in its insistence that basic human dignity be upheld in the most horrific circumstances. articles.title: The Call for Working-Class Liberalism Is Coming From Inside the House
articles.author: Gerard Di Trolio
articles.content_excerpt: The socialist left has a vexed relationship with major economists. This is a problem, because it sometimes leaves the Left on the outside of contemporary economic debates. Daron Acemoglu is precisely the sort of economist that the Left should not ignore. Alongside his frequent collaborators Simon Johnson and James A. Robinson, he is a 2024 Nobel laureate in economics. He is also among the world’s most cited economists. His new book, What Happened to Liberal Democracy? , has already received lot of attention, as his recent spat with The Economist shows. Acemoglu’s work can be summed up in the proposition that institutions matter for economic growth. He identifies two types of institutions. articles.title: Donald Trump’s Imperialism of Decline Is a Global Menace
articles.author: Atul Kohli
articles.content_excerpt: To make sense of US foreign policy under Donald Trump, we need to see it against the long-term historical background. Trump’s approach to world affairs may be erratic, but that does not mean it is completely without precedent. The United States has long been an imperial power. While not establishing formal colonies, the US has instead created an informal empire in which obsequious governments in the Global South enable the pursuit of American political and economic interests. Throughout its history, American imperialism has come in three varieties: hard militarism, covert regime change, and multilateral coercion. articles.title: The Fate of the Rohingyas Is Crucial for Myanmar’s Future
articles.author: Sushovan Dhar
articles.content_excerpt: In August 2024, Rohingya families gathered on the banks of the Naf River in Maungdaw, waiting to cross into Bangladesh as the fighting closed in. Drones and mortars found them there. Roughly two hundred people were killed , another entry in a catalogue of atrocity the Rohingya have been forced to keep for decades. What made this massacre different was who stood accused of it. The killing was attributed not to the Myanmar military, the army that drove three-quarters of a million Rohingya into exile in 2017, but to the Arakan Army , the ethnic Rakhine force that has spent the past two years dismantling that same military’s grip on the state. articles.title: The Rise of Germany’s Far Right Reflects a Systemic Crisis
articles.author: Gábor Scheiring
articles.content_excerpt: After the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) scored 44 percent of the vote in the September 6 state election in Saxony-Anhalt, many analysts sought some single, clearly identifiable reason. The interest in the AfD’s success is well justified: what happens in Germany shapes Europe and even world politics, and most mainstream accounts seek tools with which the center can disarm the far right. In this vein, the AfD’s success is said to owe to a sluggish bureaucracy, the peculiar political culture of the former East Germany, or more simply to immigration. Yet the reliance on a single explanatory factor yields single-variable strategies in response, and such strategies are bound to fail. articles.title: WFTU Statement on the 26th of July 2026 On the 73rd Anniversary of the Attack on the Moncada Barracks
articles.author: admin
articles.content_excerpt: The World Federation of Trade Unions (WFTU) salutes the heroic Cuban people on the occasion of the 73rd anniversary of the attack on the Moncada Barracks. The 26th of July remains a historic milestone in the struggle of the peoples against exploitation and imperialist domination. The heroic action led by Fidel Castro and his comrades in Santiago de Cuba marked the beginning of the revolutionary process that culminated in the triumph of the Cuban Revolution and inspired generations of workers and peoples throughout the world. The ideals of sovereignty, social justice, internationalism and workers’ dignity that emerged from Moncada continue to illuminate the struggles of the international working class today.
